trajectory_summary: The call opens on a mismatched contact and a wrong-utility guess, drifts through an unusually long bill-navigation stretch that nonetheless ends in a successful usage-graph capture, and closes with a booked in-person estimate. Energy is mixed: friction is real but self-resolving, largely because the customer (and his wife, off-line) stayed cooperative throughout rather than because the rep actively built trust or urgency.

observed_outcome.quote: Ten ten to eleven, you know, I can do it through. To eleven.
observed_outcome.reasoning: A specific day (Monday) and time window (10-11) are locked for an in-person visit, and the rep confirms the company name and follow-up text, but the wife/co-owner who holds account knowledge is never explicitly confirmed to be present.

bill_anchor_audit.bill_quote: My bills over the last year are between 155 and 196.
bill_anchor_audit.reasoning: The rep acknowledges the number ('Okay') and immediately moves to the next verify item (kilowatt usage history) without ever tying the $155-196 range back to urgency or emotional alignment against the utility; the flip line should have landed right after 04:20, e.g., referencing that range as the reason to lock in savings before the estimate.

interest_reason_audit.reasoning: The rep never asks what interested the customer in solar at any point in the call, and because the form-filler (the wife) is largely off-line for most of the conversation, no organic reason surfaces either.

primary_coaching_focus.topic: Confirming the actual lead/homeowner before running verify
primary_coaching_focus.quote: Well, I just had a few questions to get started on the estimate. Is that correct? What are your questions?
primary_coaching_focus.why: The call starts with the wrong household member and the rep never explicitly re-confirms who the applicant is or secures the wife's presence for the booked appointment; this is one of several contributing threads (along with the mid-call handoff and the scam-check moment) that kept the call from feeling fully anchored, not the sole cause of friction.

key_moments.quote: This is Bucky with Ion. I'm reaching out about the solar form you filled out online. How are you doing?
key_moments.stewart_read: The intro follows the standard template (company name + form reference) but gives no additional context (state, program framing) before the customer immediately disclaims having filled out the form, so the legitimacy anchor is thin exactly when it is tested.

key_moments.quote: Well, I just had a few questions to get started on the estimate. Is that correct? What are your questions?
key_moments.stewart_read: The customer just said he didn't submit the form and his wife likely did; the rep doesn't pause to confirm who the actual homeowner/lead is or loop the wife in immediately, instead pushing forward with the husband as if he were the applicant.

key_moments.quote: Well, I'd have to look on my phone. Just a minute.
key_moments.stewart_read: The bill/usage retrieval stretches from roughly 02:33 to 07:07 -- long relative to a typical call -- but this is not the elderly/landline failure pattern the schema flags for a 2-minute pivot; the customer is actively navigating and ultimately produces the exact usage graph needed, so the length reflects normal friction on an unfamiliar utility portal rather than a dead-end path.

key_moments.quote: I'm running your text through a, an AI system to find out whether you're real or bullshit.
key_moments.stewart_read: This is a live scam-anxiety signal about the rep's own text link, arising mid-task rather than at intro. The schema calls for an appointment-reframe response to this kind of anxiety; instead the rep answers in kind with a joke ('sometimes AI doesn't agree') and moves on without a legitimacy reassurance or reframing the appointment as customer-initiated.
